summary: Gives an overview of the third version of the Internet-Standard Management Framework, known as SNMPv3, and how it builds on SNMPv1 and SNMPv2. It explains the modular design meant to let the framework evolve, and points to the documents that make it up, including their applicability.

eli5.summary: SNMPv3 is a set of rules for checking on and controlling network gadgets from far away. This note is the table of contents and big-picture map showing how all the pieces fit together.

questions: what is the difference between snmpv2c and snmpv3
subtitle: The roadmap to SNMPv3: how the management framework fits together, and why the older versions were retired.

tldr.problem: SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 had no real security, and the documents describing the management framework were spread across many RFCs with no single guide to them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3410 gives a tutorial overview of the SNMPv3 Framework: a modular design with a data definition language, MIB modules, protocol operations, and a new security and administration layer. It summarizes each document in the set and states the status of the older versions.
tldr.outcome: The document recommends SNMPv3 over SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c, and recommends that RFCs 1157, 1441, 1901, 1909 and 1910 be reclassified as Historic. It obsoletes RFC 2570.

facts.value: 5 (Command Generator, Command Responder, Notification Originator, Notification Receiver, Proxy Forwarder)

today: RFC 3410 is Informational and, per the metadata, obsoletes RFC 2570; nothing lists it as obsoleted or updated. It remains a roadmap whose detailed content lives in the documents it points to, such as RFC 3411 and RFC 3414.

sections.title: What This Document Is For
sections.content:
RFC 3410 is an Informational introduction to the third version of the Internet-Standard Management Framework, called SNMPv3. It does not specify an Internet standard of any kind. It has three purposes: to describe how the SNMPv3 specifications relate to the SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 frameworks, to act as a roadmap to the many documents involved, and to give an easy-to-read summary of each one.

The RFC says plainly that it is tutorial and may occasionally oversimplify. If it conflicts with the detailed documents, the detailed documents prevail. It was produced by the SNMPv3 Working Group of the IETF.
sections.eli5: This is a guidebook, not the rulebook. If the guidebook and a rulebook disagree, the rulebook wins.

sections.title: The Shared Framework Structure
sections.content:
All three versions share one basic structure. An enterprise has several managed nodes, each with an SNMP entity that gives remote access to management instrumentation (traditionally called an agent). It has at least one SNMP entity running management applications (typically called a manager). A management protocol carries management information between them.

The architecture is modular and has four parts: a data definition language, definitions of management information (the Management Information Base, or MIB), a protocol definition, and security and administration. The RFC explains that the data definition language and MIB were made independent of the protocol, so the protocol could be replaced without redefining the information. That was meant to ease a move to OSI-based management. The RFC says history showed this was the right decision for the wrong reason: it eased the moves from SNMPv1 to SNMPv2 and from SNMPv2 to SNMPv3 instead.
sections.eli5: Think of a school with a few helpers in every classroom and a principal who asks them questions. The question-asking rules, the list of things you can ask about, and the lock on the door are kept as separate pieces so any one can be swapped out.

sections.title: SNMPv1, SNMPv2 and the Road to SNMPv3
sections.content:
SNMPv1 is defined by STD 16 (RFC 1155 and RFC 1212), STD 15 (RFC 1157, the protocol), and companions such as MIB-II (RFC 1213) and RFC 1215 for traps. Its protocol operators are get, get-next, get-response, set-request and trap. Its security was a trivial authentication scheme based on community strings, which the RFC calls a known fundamental weakness.

SNMPv2 added expanded data types (for example a 64 bit counter), the get-bulk operator, a confirmed notification called inform, richer error handling, and improved sets. But it was incomplete: it did not deliver the security and administration its designers wanted, meaning authentication, privacy, access control and remote configuration. Different security efforts (SNMPv2c, SNMPv2u and SNMPv2*) went along with it. SNMPv2c had the most IETF support but no security, while SNMPv2u and SNMPv2* had security but lacked consensus.

The SNMPv3 Working Group was chartered to merge the ideas of SNMPv2u and SNMPv2* into one specification. It reused the SNMPv2 Draft Standard documents (RFCs 1902 through 1908) for everything outside security and administration. The RFC summarizes the result as SNMPv2 with additional security and administration capabilities.
sections.eli5: The first two versions were like a house with no lock on the front door. Version 3 kept the house and added a proper lock, a key system, and rules about who may enter which room.

sections.title: The SNMPv3 Document Set
sections.content:
The first three parts of the SNMPv3 Framework are taken from SNMPv2, and the security and administration documents are new. The RFC lists them:

  • RFC 3411 describes the overall architecture, with emphasis on security and administration.
  • RFC 3412 covers message processing and dispatching, so one engine can support multiple message processing models.
  • RFC 3413 describes the five application types: Command Generators, Command Responders, Notification Originators, Notification Receivers and Proxy Forwarders.
  • RFC 3414 defines the User-based Security Model (USM).
  • RFC 3415 defines the View-based Access Control Model (VACM).
  • RFC 2576 covers coexistence with SNMPv1 and SNMPv2.

Outside that list, the data definition language is SMIv2 (STD 58, RFCs 2578 to 2580), protocol operations are in RFC 3416, and transport mappings are in RFC 3417. The UDP mapping is the preferred one, and systems that use other mappings should also provide proxy service to the UDP mapping. RFC 3418 defines managed objects describing an SNMP entity.

The RFC notes that management information from any MIB module can generally be used with any protocol version. The exception is the Counter64 type, which an SNMPv1-only engine cannot convey. As of writing, it counts more than 100 standards-track MIB modules with over 10,000 objects.
sections.eli5: SNMPv3 is a binder of small booklets. One explains the big picture, one explains how messages are sorted, one explains the kinds of helpers, one explains the passwords and locks, and one explains who may see what.

sections.title: Security and Access Control in SNMPv3
sections.content:
The User-based Security Model defends against four threats: modification of information, masquerade, message stream modification and disclosure. It uses MD5 and the Secure Hash Algorithm as keyed hashing algorithms to protect data integrity, and loosely synchronized monotonically increasing time indicators against message stream modification. For disclosure protection it uses DES in cipher block chaining mode. Support for DES is optional, primarily because export and usage restrictions in many countries make cryptographic products hard to ship and use. The RFC says work was underway to specify AES for the USM as a separate document.

All USM protocols rely on pre-placed (private) keys. The architecture permits public key mechanisms, but at the time of writing no SNMPv3 security model on the standards track used them. VACM provides view-based access control and can run alongside several message processing models and security models in one engine.

The RFC adds one operational warning: configure SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c access no more generously than unauthenticated SNMPv3 access. Its image is not guarding the front door with armed guards while leaving the back door open. Its own security section says that, as a roadmap, it introduces no new security considerations.
sections.eli5: Version 3 can check that a message really came from who it says and was not changed, and can scramble it so snoopers cannot read it. It also keeps a list of which people may look at which things.

sections.title: Standardization Status of the Older Versions
sections.content:
SMIv1 (STD 16) became a full Standard in 1990 and stayed one even after SMIv2 reached full Standard, but it is not recommended. It could not be made Historic without making the standards-track documents that depend on it Historic too. The RFC says the IETF requires new MIB modules to use SMIv2.

SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c carry only plain-text community strings and are therefore fundamentally insecure. The RFC says that when the SNMPv3 security specifications reached full Standard, SNMPv1 (formerly STD 15) and SNMPv2c (RFC 1901) were declared Historic to send a clear message that SNMPv3 is the framework of choice. The IETF process does not control what vendors build or users deploy, and the RFC expects multi-lingual products supporting SNMPv1 or SNMPv2c alongside SNMPv3 to continue.

The working group recommends that RFCs 1157, 1441, 1901, 1909 and 1910 be reclassified as Historical documents.
sections.eli5: The old versions are like a diary with a flimsy lock. People may still use them, but the experts say to switch to the sturdy one.
